literature.
Description: As Lunularia cruciata has been described and illustrated frequently in the
literature (e.g. Scott 1985, Schuster 1992b, Atherton et al. 2010), no description or illustration is
given here.
Illustrations: Scott (1985, Figures 31, 32); Schuster (1992b, Figure 00; Atherton et al. (2010,
page 252).
Habitat: Soil and weathered rock in damp to wet situations subject to seasonal drying.
Distribution on LHI: Settlement, north-eastern slopes of Mt Lidgbird, northern face of Mt
Gower.
Total distribution: Temperate and subtropical regions of the world.
Discussion: Lunularia cruciata is probably the most recognisable of all liverwort species
because of its distinctive lunate gemmae cups. It was introduced into Australia in the late 19th
century and has since spread widely in southern Australia, reaching as far north as Carnarvon
Gorge in southern Queensland (Meagher 2015). Sporophytes are uncommon, so that dispersal is
probably mostly if not entirely by gemmae or thallus fragments.
The first collection of the species on Lord Howe Island was made by Cliff Beauglehole in 1962,
and a further three collections were made by Elizabeth Brown in the 2000s. Despite its ubiquity
and ease of identification, it was not found in the current study.

Marchantiaceae Lindl.
The family Marchantiaceae includes three genera, of which only Marchantia is known from
Australia, New Zealand and New Caledonia. Only Marchantia is known for Lord Howe Island.

Marchantia L.
This genus of 26 species (Bischler 1989) is represented in Australia and New Zealand by five
species. Only Marchantia berteroana and M. pileata occur on Lord Howe Island. They can be
separated by the following key:

Marchantia berteroana Lehm. & Lindenb.
Marchantia berteroana Lehm. & Lindenb., Nov. Stirp. Pug. 4: 32 (1832)
Type: NEW ZEALAND, ‘Makororo River, Ahuriri, etc.’ Colenso s.n., date unknown,
herbarium location unknown; Auckland, Sinclair s.n., date unknown, herbarium unknown.
Description: This species has been described comprehensively by Scott (1985), Bischler (1989)
and Perold (1995).
Illustrations: Scott (1985, Figure 28), Bischler (1989, Figure 3), Perold (1995, Figure 4).
Habitat: Soil in damp situations.
Distribution on LHI: Eastern slopes of Mt Lidgbird, Erskine Valley, summit plateau of Mt
Gower.
Total distribution: Temperate regions of the southern hemisphere.
Discussion: Stephani (1889) first reported this species from Lord Howe Island, as Marchantia
cephaloscypha, based on a collection by Fullagar. Bischler (1989) noted that all reports of
M. polymorpha L. from New Caledonia were M. berteroana.

Marchantia pileata Mitt.
Marchantia pileata Mitt., Fl. Nov-Zel. 2: 169 (1855)
Type: NEW ZEALAND, Makororo River, Colenso s.n., date unknown, herbarium unknown.
Description: This species has been described comprehensively by Bischler (1989).
Illustrations: Bischler (1989, Figure 10).
Habitat: Soil in damp situations.
Distribution on LHI: Erskine Valley and eastern slopes of Intermediate Hill and Mt Lidgbird.
Total distribution: Australia (Tas, Vic, ACT, NSW, Qld, LHI), New Zealand.

                                                                               174
Discussion: Marchantia pileata is a common species in eastern Australia and New Zealand
(Bischler 1989), although often misidentified as M. foliacea in Australia because it was not
treated by Scott (1985). Specimens from Lord Howe Island previously identified as Marchantia
foliacea Mitt. were found to be M. pileata in this study. M. pileata does not extend to New
Caledonia; Bischler (1989) found that all records from there were referable to M. emarginata
var. lecordiana.

                                                                             Introduction


species, but these gemmae are usually difficult to see with only a hand lens. Larger
gemmae may also develop in specialised gemmae cups on the dorsal surface, as in
Marchantia berteroana and Lunularia cruciata. •
     Most thallose liverworts are prostrate or dendroid, so the distinction between the
dorsal and ventral surfaces will be obvious. If there is any doubt, the ventral surface
is usually dull rather than shiny, and in prostrate species the rhizoids will be attached
to the ventral surface.
    Male and female structures and sporophytes are basically the same as those of
leafy liverworts. The exceptions are the hornworts (Megaceros, Phaeoceros and their
allies), in which the capsule is like a thick needle standing erect on the surface of the
thallus.

Leafy liverworts                                                                   ..
The nature of the leaves is the primary diagnostic feature for separating one_ species
from another, and also for distinguishing liverworts in general from mosses. Liverwort
leaves always lack a costa, and are almost always arranged in two or three rows on the
stem. When leaves are paired they grow on opposite sides of the stem. \3/hen in
threes, the third row is usually attached along the vE:ntral surface; the leaves of this_
row are called underleaves. These are usually smaller than the other leaves and h�ve
a different shape. Some species have underleaves that can be so small as to be
undetectable with a hand lens. In the key, these specie� (e.g. Cephaloziella exiliflora)
will key out as 'without underleaves'. A few species, such as Chiloscyphus muricatus,
have minute, spike-like papillae on the leaves which c·an give the leaves a roughened
appearance under a hand lens.
    The angle between the leaves and stem at the point of attachment (called the leaf
insertion) is an important diagnostic feature for many_genera and species. The three
major types of leaf insertion are 'transverse', 'incubous' and 'succubous' (see· the
illustration on the next page).
    Transverse leaves are inserted at right angles to the stem axis, so that an imaginary
stream of water directed onto the leaves from the dorsal side would pass straight
between the leaves. Succubous leaves have the lower (ventral) end of the insertion
closest to the apex of the stem, so that a stream of water would run down the shoot
like water running over roof tiles. Incubous leaves are tilted in the.opposite direction,
